title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Sandworm and Qilin are inside Cisco firewall management consoles — and the federal deadline on the patch is tomorrow
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild, and Cisco Talos has since set out what the exploitation actually looks like. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass at CVSS 10.0, caused by an improper system process created at boot: a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and added indicators of compromise in late July without flagging exploitation, then updated the advisory on 9 September to say it became aware of active exploitation in August. Talos now describes three distinct intrusion clusters abusing CVE-2026-20079 together with the lower-severity CVE-2026-20316: UAT-12197, which drops JSP web shells and Java command executors to harvest credentials; UAT-11823, which deployed Netcat reverse shells and a variant of Cyclops Blink, a modular ELF implant previously attributed to the Russian state-sponsored group Sandworm, for credential harvesting and network reconnaissance; and UAT-11988, which used FMC’s own built-in tooling for reconnaissance, credential theft and security-tool termination before deploying Qilin ransomware on selected systems. CISA added the flaw to the KEV catalog on 9 September with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September — tomorrow. Read this carefully for what it is and is not. No OT or ICS impact has been reported, and no critical-infrastructure victim has been named; what is documented is compromise of network security management infrastructure. But FMC is the console that configures the firewalls enforcing the boundary between your corporate network and generation, substation and DER control networks, and Sandworm is the actor with the longest record of causing electricity outages. Espionage and ransomware converging on the same management appliance is the part worth acting on.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek, with cluster detail corroborated by The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; federal deadline 12 Sep 2026

items.title: Fire Ant turns Cisco routers and TACACS servers into listening posts inside critical-infrastructure networks
items.content_text: Sygnia published findings on 30 August that the China-nexus group it tracks as Fire Ant has moved past VMware hypervisors into the network layer itself, compromising Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts inside a large interconnected environment. On the routers it ran an implant that suppressed selected syslog messages, opened outbound sessions and served interactive shells with no logging. On TACACS it injected a library into the running daemon and copied administrator credentials as sessions were accepted. Sygnia says the group used that position to scan and attempt connections into linked critical-infrastructure networks, without confirming compromise there. For an electricity operator the uncomfortable part is the ordering: routers and TACACS are what your control-centre audit trail rests on, so if they are lying, every downstream log inherits the lie.
tags: Incident — Network and authentication tier compromise

items.title: FBI seizes the Chinese state-sponsored scanning and relay platforms that had been mapping US critical infrastructure
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of two linked platforms, QScan and QTRouter, operated by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan was the reconnaissance side; QTRouter relayed traffic through compromised third-party routers and IoT devices so intrusions appeared to originate from ordinary domestic addresses. Because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware for command and authentication, both platforms are now inoperable. Named victims are federal — NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy and others — and activity dates to at least 2018. For an electricity operator the takeaway is the relay layer: the source addresses in your firewall logs were never a reliable signal of who was on the other end.

items.title: UK government confirms a cyberattack took a generator offline — and the affected site sat below the regulated reporting threshold
items.content_text: The UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has confirmed on the record that a cyber incident affected a small-scale energy generator, while stating the wider energy system was never at risk. It is the first publicly acknowledged cyberattack on a British generating asset. The four-day outage figure and the attribution to Iran-linked actors come from Sunday Telegraph sourcing rather than an official statement, and the NCSC declined to comment. No plant, operator, technology or access route has been published. The operationally significant detail is that the NCSC logged no outage reports from regulated power station operators, which places the affected site beneath the reporting regime — and the embedded generation, CHP, standby and storage estate is numerous, frequently unmanned, and commonly reached through vendor remote access.
tags: Incident — Confirmed cyberattack on a generating asset

items.title: CERT Polska: an attacker crossed a shared private cellular network from a wind farm into a heating plant and stopped its turbine
items.content_text: CERT Polska’s follow-up report describes an intrusion that began at a wind farm and ended at an unrelated combined heat and power plant, with the turbine taken out of service. The bridge was a private APN both operators bought from the same carrier. A private APN is a billing and addressing construct, not a security boundary: if devices on it can address one another, one operator’s compromised cellular router becomes another operator’s ingress path. For anyone running distributed generation over carrier links — wind, solar, storage, district energy, remote substations — this is the clearest published example of an attack path most operators have never asked their carrier about.
tags: Incident — Lateral movement between unrelated operators

items.title: Berlin refused to pay, and the published dump reportedly includes critical-infrastructure vulnerability analyses
items.content_text: Rhysida released the data it took from Berlin’s state administration on 4 September after the city declined a demand reported at 30 bitcoin. The claimed set runs to roughly 5.79 TB across about 1.44 million files and, alongside personnel and payroll records, is reported to contain vulnerability analyses covering the city’s water supply plus plaintext credentials for municipal systems including a building atlas, a payments database and administrator accounts. The city’s own account has data leaving from 7 August and continuing to around 12 August, with the affected departments not physically disconnected until 14 August. For a utility the transferable point is not the ransomware — it is that the documents which describe how to hurt you frequently sit somewhere you do not control: with a regulator, a municipal owner, an engineering consultancy or an interconnection partner.
tags: Incident — Government breach exposes critical-infrastructure risk documentation

items.title: Treasury sanctions an Iranian intelligence-directed network it says has been exfiltrating data from US energy companies since 2023
items.content_text: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security-directed hacking network on 24 August as part of a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels; the State Department posted a related reward notice. Treasury states the network has breached and exfiltrated data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. Read the scope carefully. What is attributed here is espionage and data theft — engineering drawings, network documentation, credentials, personnel records — not manipulation of generation or transmission equipment. The reason a utility should still care is conversion: access collected for espionage becomes disruption capability the moment tasking changes, and the vendor accounts and remote-management paths described here are the same ones a disruptive operator would inherit.
tags: Incident — Nation-state targeting of energy companies

items.title: DOE and Sandia put a language model on the least glamorous part of grid detection: preparing the data
items.content_text: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security and Emergency Response and Sandia National Laboratories reported on 8 September on C2E2, a tool developed under the AI-FORTS programme that uses large language models to automate the data-engineering step in cyber-physical threat detection for the electric grid. The point is not that a model spots the attack. It is that turning heterogeneous SCADA, relay, PMU and network telemetry into a form a detection model can consume normally takes a specialist roughly two months per deployment; Sandia reports cutting that to hours, with around 95% accuracy in detecting and localising simulated threats in testing. That matters for utilities because data preparation, not algorithm choice, is what has stalled most anomaly-detection projects at the pilot stage. Sandia is clear this has not yet been trialled at an operating utility, and the next phase specifically targets hallucination-driven false or missed detections — a failure mode a control room cannot tolerate.

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — AI-assisted grid threat detection
_otthreatfeed.source_name: DOE CESER and Sandia National Laboratories, reported by Industrial Cyber
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Reported 8 Sep 2026

items.title: The campaign that hit water is now probing energy control systems — and there is a $10 million bounty attached to it
items.content_text: Reporting on 2 September said Iranian government-linked operators have widened their targeting beyond the water sector to telecommunications networks and energy providers, concentrating on internet-exposed automated control systems. Officials quoted describe attempted intrusions rather than confirmed operational impact so far, and that distinction is worth holding on to. Separately, on 3 September the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme offered up to $10 million for information on an IRGC-affiliated figure it links to the campaign against US critical infrastructure. For a generation or transmission operator the useful detail is the access pattern rather than the actor: the water intrusions ran through controllers and cellular-connected devices reachable from the public internet with weak or default authentication, not through any novel exploit. The equivalent exposure here is unmanned substations, remote generation and DER sites, and standing vendor maintenance links.
tags: Targeting — Iran-linked campaign widens beyond water into telecommunications and energy; attempts reported, no confirmed OT impact

items.title: Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
items.content_text: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a utility the honest question is what your detection-to-containment interval actually is between the corporate boundary and the control centre, and whether it survives an adversary working at machine pace overnight.
tags: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index and the report “The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker”, reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor-published research; the figures are the authors’ own test results and have not been independently reproduced

items.title: GRIDLOCK: modelling puts a 92% chance of a major attack on UK battery storage by 2031 — and 29% of the fleet is enough
items.content_text: Centrii published its GRIDLOCK report on 3 September, modelling what happens when an adversary uses grid-connected battery storage as the weapon rather than the target. In the scenario, compromised BESS units are commanded to swing output in concert, manipulating physical power flows to destabilise system frequency rather than saturating a network link — the report frames it as a grid-scale denial of service delivered in energy. Across 10,000 Monte Carlo runs against three security postures, Centrii puts the probability of a major attack on UK battery storage by 2031 at 92%, and calculates that compromising roughly 29% of national capacity — on the order of 400 units — could be enough to trigger a nationwide outage affecting 67 million people, with costs modelled up to £10 billion. Mandatory certification and regular attack-readiness drills cut that probability to 61% and push the earliest likely window from 2027 to 2028. A parallel run on Texas returns the same 92% figure by 2031, with economic damage modelled up to $65 billion. This is modelling rather than a reported incident, and its value is in the premise it tests: a large amount of fast-acting capacity dispatched from a small number of control planes.

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat Intelligence — Scenario modelling
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Centrii GRIDLOCK report — reported by Industrial Cyber and New Civil Engineer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Six steps to being able to disconnect — and a planning horizon of three months running islanded
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. The step that changes the engineering is the second-to-last one — keeping monitoring alive after you cut the link, since an isolation plan that also blinds the control room is not one anyone will execute. The addition worth arguing about internally is the planning horizon: Nozomi suggests operators assume they may need to sustain isolated operations for up to three months. For generation and transmission that pushes the question past network design and into spares, licence servers, time synchronisation and how long an EMS can run without its enterprise dependencies.

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

items.title: A hostile battery dispatch looks identical to a profitable one — and very few control planes can order it
items.content_text: Help Net Security published an analysis on 2 September, built on modelling from Rafael Narezzi of the London firm Centrii, arguing that grid-connected battery energy storage has concentrated an unusual amount of fast-acting power behind a small number of cloud control planes. Batteries earn revenue by responding to frequency in under a second, so on a control room screen a hostile coordinated swing and a legitimate revenue-driven one look the same — the frequency trace alone tells the operator nothing about intent. Control is also pooled: third-party optimisers and manufacturer cloud platforms dispatch fleets spread across many sites and several balancing areas, which means the meaningful unit of risk is the platform, not the individual site. This is analysis and modelling rather than a reported incident, and it is worth reading as a design question about who can issue a fleet-wide setpoint and what would notice if someone else did.

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat Intelligence — Analysis
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Help Net Security interview and analysis with Centrii
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Researchers used an AI model to port a working PLC exploit to a second controller — then bricked it
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. The honest read for a utility is narrow but real: this does not create new exploits, it lowers the cost of spreading an existing one across the model variants sitting in your substations and generating sites.

items.title: NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating that it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, carried out by a range of threat actors, and that the activity has resulted in some limited real-world disruption. It names no victims, actors or techniques. What makes it worth reading in a control room is the framing: the NCSC tells organisations not to assume their OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. For an electricity operator that is a direct description of the embedded generation, storage and unmanned substation estate — the sites commissioned by an integrator, connected over a carrier link, and never re-surveyed. It lands three days after DESNZ confirmed a UK generator was taken offline by a cyberattack.
tags: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

items.title: Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers across the energy sector
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to turn a well-documented open-source S7 library into custom tooling that queries internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers and blends in as legitimate monitoring traffic. The agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning rather than manipulation, and they name energy among the targeted sectors. The significant claim is not a new exploit — it is that protocol-level expertise is no longer the barrier it was. Familiarity with S7comm, DNP3 or IEC 61850 used to gate who could write working ICS tooling; it no longer does, and the population of people able to interrogate an exposed controller has grown accordingly.
tags: Threat intel — Joint federal advisory on ICS protocol tooling

items.title: CISA ran the same attack against two critical-infrastructure organisations — one caught it, the other never noticed
items.content_text: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes the results of red-team assessments at a water and wastewater entity and a government organisation, run with comparable tradecraft. One organisation detected and responded; the other did not notice a domain compromise. The report is unusually direct about why. The difference was not tooling budget — both had capable products deployed — but whether anyone was reviewing what those products produced, whether identity events were correlated, and whether the team had practised the response. For a utility running an EMS or SCADA domain alongside a corporate one, the transferable finding is that Active Directory abuse and living-off-the-land movement generated telemetry in both cases; only one organisation acted on it.
tags: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings

items.title: Siemens patches an authentication bypass in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays, the gear that trips your feeders
items.content_text: Siemens ProductCERT published SSA-142885 on 8 September, covering fourteen vulnerabilities in the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relay family across every firmware version before V2.70. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS 9.8, is an information disclosure in the device web interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker calculate current and previous session identifiers and step straight past authentication. Two companion issues make that worse: weak session-token entropy in CVE-2026-62646, and a role-based access control bypass in CVE-2026-62650 that hands an attacker administrative rights. A pre-authentication denial-of-service condition is also fixed. Siemens reports no exploitation, and no change of state was found when the advisory was re-checked on 11 September. This remains the highest-consequence unexploited item on the board for transmission and distribution operators because of placement rather than score — 7SR5 relays sit in feeder, transformer and busbar protection schemes, and Siemens took the unusual step of reminding TSOs and DSOs to confirm their redundant secondary protection is healthy.
tags: Critical Advisory — Protection relay, no known exploitation

items.title: “MikroTrick” moves from disclosed to confirmed exploited — two CVSS 9.2 SSH flaws hand over RouterOS admin
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerability chain known as “MikroTrick” — disclosed earlier but not previously confirmed as exploited — is now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device. A third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors; it noted only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. That is the honest boundary of this item — there is no confirmed utility victim and no confirmed OT impact. It earns a place here because of where this hardware tends to live in an electricity network: cheap, capable routers are a common choice for cellular or fixed-wireless backhaul at unmanned substations, distributed generation sites and storage compounds, often installed by a contractor and often the one device on that site with a route to both the corporate network and the RTU.
tags: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-site edge routers

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-site edge routers

items.title: CISA’s 8 September KEV batch is led by a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform your MSP uses
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September, all with vendor fixes already available. The one that matters most to utilities is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, scored CVSS 10.0: a static code injection weakness giving pre-authentication remote code execution on the remote monitoring and management server. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal remediation deadline is 11 September. RMM platforms are a recurring bridge into OT-adjacent networks at MSP-managed generating stations, substations and DER sites, because the agent runs with high privilege on the very hosts that reach engineering systems. The batch also carries two exploited Windows privilege-escalation zero-days, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, plus an Adobe Commerce template-injection flaw.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026

items.title: September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens ships nine advisories, Schneider four, with a distribution RTU fix in the pile
items.content_text: The 8 September ICS patch round landed heavier than usual for electricity operators. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven of them on the day, with critical findings in the Reyrolle 7SR5 relay family covered separately above, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT, and began rolling out fixes for Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 at CVSS 7.8 across affected product lines. Schneider Electric published four. The most severe is a critical authentication vulnerability in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2. Closer to the grid edge, Schneider also fixed a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300 — the former Easergy T300 RTU used for MV feeder automation and substation remote terminal duty — alongside EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert and a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Aveva disclosed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, and CISA published them on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: CVE-2026-81821, a hardcoded cryptographic key, and CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing, both at CVSS 8.4, alongside a missing-authorisation issue at 5.3 and a cross-site scripting flaw at 4.7, all fixed in Pipeline Integrity Monitor 2025 SP1 P2. Nothing in the round is reported as exploited, and that remained true when the batch was re-checked on 11 September. The T300 item is covered separately below.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday

items.title: The one genuinely new power item this cycle is a feeder-automation RTU — Schneider’s PowerLogic T300
items.content_text: Schneider Electric’s September 2026 patch release included a high-severity vulnerability in the PowerLogic T300 platform, the rebranded Easergy T300 remote terminal unit used for MV distribution feeder automation and monitoring. It is a separate advisory from the Modicon M580 critical flaw (CVE-2026-3869) and the Siemens Reyrolle 7SR5 relay set published in the same cycle, and it is the only genuinely new electricity-sector disclosure found in the 9–11 September window. Be clear about what is and is not known: the secondary reporting reviewed — SecurityWeek’s ICS Patch Tuesday round-up and the associated conference coverage — characterised the severity only as “high” and did not carry a CVE identifier or a CVSS vector, so none is published here. A vendor fix or mitigation was issued as part of the same September advisory cycle. No exploitation has been reported. The reason it matters out of proportion to a missing score is the device’s job: a T300 sits in a ring main unit or pole-mounted cabinet and actuates switchgear, so it is one of the few products in this month’s pile that can directly change the state of a distribution feeder.
tags: Advisory — Distribution feeder RTU, no known exploitation

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — Distribution feeder RTU, no known exploitation

items.title: CISA’s 3 September batch lands on remote access and the firmware tool — IXON VPN client, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
items.content_text: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September. Three are worth an operator’s attention. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client, where CVE-2026-75925 lets an attacker achieve remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — that machine is usually an engineer’s laptop or a jump host that already holds a route into substation and plant networks. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 allows commands or code to run at the permission level of the logged-in user; ControlFLASH is the tool used to push firmware to relays, controllers and communication modules, so the account running it is normally privileged. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects — relevant wherever Ignition fronts an EMS or generation SCADA layer. None is reported as exploited.

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected.

items.title: CISA’s 1 September ICS batch is mostly Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight industrial control system advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The one most sites will notice first is ICSA-26-244-01, covering four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625. All four are remotely triggerable with no authentication and no user interaction: a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet crashes the RSLinx Classic service. Rockwell has fixed all four in version 4.60. The rest of the batch covers the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (ICSA-26-244-02), the Logix platform (-03, reaching ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). No exploitation has been reported for any of them.

items.title: A print server chained to unauthenticated code execution — PaperCut’s zero-day pair lands in KEV
items.content_text: PaperCut confirmed on 27 August that it was investigating active exploitation of its NG and MF print-management products, and assigned CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 the following day. The first lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the Application Server and change its configuration; the second turns that change into arbitrary code execution through unsafe reflection. Chained, they give a network-adjacent attacker code execution with no credentials at all, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 31 August. Print management almost never appears on an OT asset register. The server usually does hold a domain service account, does sit on the same segment as engineering workstations, and is reachable from nearly every host in the estate — which makes it a convenient staging point rather than a target in its own right. Arctic Wolf reported on 6 September that it is seeing the chain used in practice: after gaining execution, operators run reconnaissance, create privileged accounts and harvest credentials and PaperCut configuration secrets — behaviour consistent with establishing a durable foothold rather than a smash-and-grab.

items.title: A protocol test set that talks directly to your field devices picks up two flaws — one of them a decade old
items.content_text: CISA’s 27 August advisory batch includes ASE2000 V2, the communications test set engineers use to exercise DNP3, IEC 60870-5 and Modbus links when commissioning or troubleshooting RTUs, relays and substation gateways. Two issues are documented in versions 2.25 through 2.37: a bundled Apache log4net component that does not disable XML external entities when parsing its configuration file (CVE-2018-1285), and improper certificate validation in 2.35 through 2.37 (CVE-2026-18717) that lets an attacker on the path impersonate the trusted peer, complete the TLS handshake and read or alter the protected traffic. The reason this belongs on a power page rather than in the noise is placement, not score: the test set runs on a laptop that is deliberately connected straight to protection and control equipment, often inside the substation fence, and it is exactly the kind of tool that travels between sites.

items.title: Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
items.content_text: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch that included NetScaler. None is an ICS product, and all three sit in the layer utilities depend on rather than the layer they regulate. The Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-53362 matters because the historian, engineering server, protocol gateway and network monitoring appliance in most substations and control centres are Linux underneath, and vendor appliances inherit kernel patches on the vendor’s schedule rather than yours. CVE-2026-66384 in JFrog Artifactory is a path-traversal issue in a build-artifact repository — relevant where firmware, HMI images or automation packages are staged before they reach the field. The ownCloud bug, CVE-2023-49105, is nearly three years old and patched, which usually means the exposed instances are ones nobody owns.

items.title: A seven-year-old SQL Server flaw is now confirmed exploited — and it is the database under your historian
items.content_text: CISA added six vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, and the one that matters most on the plant floor is CVE-2019-1068, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft SQL Server patched in July 2019 and only now confirmed as exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation runs code under the SQL Server Database Engine service account; where that account is over-privileged — which is common on systems installed by an integrator years ago — the attacker moves off the database and onto the Windows host. In a utility the exposure sits in the historian and the reporting tier behind the EMS or DMS — PI interfaces, outage-management reporting, relay event archives and metering data warehouses are commonly backed by a SQL Server instance an integrator built years ago and no one has revisited, and it usually lives in the corporate-facing part of the environment rather than deep in the substation network. No public write-up of the in-the-wild technique has appeared, so detection guidance is thin; the federal remediation deadline is 29 August. Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 was added in the same batch.

items.title: The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from “patch soon” to confirmed in-the-wild exploitation. The flaw is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August, following publication of a technical analysis and proof of concept. Federal agencies must remediate by 29 August. For utilities, NetScaler frequently fronts the remote access that engineering, control-centre and vendor staff use to reach OT. Exploitation has not tailed off: reporting on 5 September describes continued attempts against the authentication bypass from multiple geolocations, so an appliance patched late should be treated as possibly already touched rather than simply late.

items.title: Two unauthenticated flaws in Veeam ONE 13 — the monitoring layer that watches the backups you would restore from
items.content_text: Veeam disclosed vulnerabilities in Veeam ONE 13 in knowledge-base articles published on 25 August. CVE-2026-64633 is rated CVSS v4.0 10.0 and allows remote, unauthenticated code execution on the Veeam ONE agent host; CVE-2026-65641 is rated 9.3 and lets a remote unauthenticated attacker coerce SMB authentication out of the Veeam ONE service account, which is the first step in relaying that account somewhere more useful. Veeam ONE 13.x is affected and the 12.x line is not. On the grid side Veeam ONE is typically the console watching backups of the EMS, historian and substation engineering workstations — the recovery capability you would need if a control-centre application had to be rebuilt. There is no report of exploitation yet, but backup and monitoring servers are a standing target precisely because compromising them removes the recovery option before the ransomware runs.

items.title: The Git server holding your PLC projects just went into KEV — Gitea is being exploited without much effort
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. The flaw, rated CVSS 9.8, lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July; exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea has quietly become common in engineering groups because it is easy to stand up inside a plant network for PLC projects, HMI screens, configuration baselines and automation scripts. That is precisely the problem: a modest contractor account becomes code execution on a server that holds the authoritative copy of your control logic. Federal remediation was due 28 August.

items.title: 117 federal reporting rules across 27 agencies — and the first hours of an incident are when they collide
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on Government Accountability Office work, counting 117 separate federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than ideological: duplicative notifications with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same small group of people away from containment during the hours when containment is most effective. Electricity operators recognise the shape of this — a single event at a registered entity can trigger E-ISAC reporting, an OE-417 to the Department of Energy, NERC CIP-008 obligations, state utility commission notification, and, for entities with federal contracts or regulated data, more besides. The analysis lands as CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn, which is the point at which harmonisation either happens or does not.

items.title: The free assessment small operators actually used is being withdrawn — and nothing at that price replaces it
items.content_text: Cybersecurity Dive reported on 3 September that CISA has told staff to stop delivering six of the free assessment services it has offered critical-infrastructure owners, including its on-site architecture design review and several facilitated risk and resilience assessments, following an internal direction reportedly given on 25 August. The agency had not published a formal notice as of this edition, so the exact scope and end dates should be read as reported rather than confirmed. The operators most affected are the ones with the least to fall back on: municipal utilities, generation and transmission co-operatives and small investor-owned utilities that used these engagements as their only external review, and for whom the commercial equivalent is a five-figure engagement not in this year’s budget.

items.title: OpenAI pledges $1bn to put frontier AI in the hands of critical-infrastructure defenders — eligibility still undefined
items.content_text: OpenAI said on 4 September that it will commit $1 billion to an initiative it calls Daybreak, offering subsidised AI cyber capabilities, training and technical assistance to defenders of critical infrastructure. Detail on cost, eligibility and what “subsidised” means in practice has not been published, and no delivery timeline has been given. For electricity operators this is worth logging rather than acting on, but it lands in a telling week: Forescout published its demonstration that a supervised model can re-target a working PLC exploit at a sibling controller in a matter of hours, so capability is accumulating on both sides of the line. If your utility is small enough that a programme like this would change what tooling you can afford, register interest early — and settle two questions before committing anything operational to it: what leaves your environment, and what happens to the capability when the subsidy ends.

items.title: Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance — and it applies to you as a service provider, not just to your suppliers
items.content_text: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It asks providers to hold a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, to send plain-language updates rather than legal boilerplate, to give affected users root-cause and technical detail they can act on, and to align messaging with legal and regulatory duties. The framing is deliberately about service providers, which is how a utility should read it in two directions at once: it is the standard to hold your EMS, metering and remote-support vendors to, and it is also the standard your customers, your balancing authority and your regulator will apply to you during an outage you cannot immediately explain.

items.title: CISA publishes internet exposure reduction guidance — and the target list for this sector is unmanned substations, distributed generation and storage sites, and the cellular-linked RTUs and gateways that sit behind them
items.content_text: CISA released guidance on 26 August directing organisations to identify which of their systems are reachable from the internet, remove remote access that is not required, and harden whatever must stay externally accessible. It is deliberately unglamorous: an inventory step, a removal step and a hardening step, published in the same week the UK NCSC warned that internet-exposed OT and edge devices are being targeted with real-world disruption already caused. Grid operators carry the widest population of remotely sited, thinly monitored equipment of any sector. The guidance is aimed squarely at the pattern that produced this month’s incidents: a controller or gateway reachable from the public internet because a carrier link, a vendor support tunnel or a decommissioned project left it that way. The guidance carries no deadline and applies to no one by force, which is precisely why it tends to be filed rather than executed.

items.title: A new executive order puts foreign-made grid equipment — including RTUs and control systems — under federal review
items.content_text: Executive Order 14420, signed 26 August, prohibits the acquisition, importation, transfer or installation of certain foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment and directs the Department of Energy to restrict, condition or unwind equipment it judges to carry sabotage, cyber, supply-disruption or catastrophic-infrastructure risk. The order is grounded in a declared national emergency over the possibility of digital backdoors built into foreign-manufactured equipment that would permit remote access and sabotage. What makes it operationally significant rather than purely political is the scope: alongside transformers, inverters and energy storage, it names industrial control systems explicitly, including remote terminal units. Countries named in reporting on the order include China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. Implementation detail, including how existing installed equipment will be treated, sits with DOE and has not yet been published.

items.title: The 2026 CIP picture: CIP-003-9 and CIP-012-2 now in force, CIP-015 internal monitoring ahead
items.content_text: Three dates define this year for registered entities. CIP-003-9 became enforceable on 1 April 2026, extending governance expectations to low-impact BES cyber systems with particular attention to vendor remote access and supply chain. CIP-012-2 took effect on 1 July 2026, tightening protection of real-time operational data exchanged between control centres. CIP-015-1 has been effective since September 2025 with phased compliance running to 2030, and introduces internal network security monitoring — east-west visibility inside the electronic security perimeter rather than only at its edge. NERC’s January 2026 CIP roadmap signals where the standards go next, including cloud, telecommunications dependency and inverter-based resources.
